problem_shape: This family is about the moment when a computer design has to become a physical thing. On screen, a surface can bend freely, pass through itself by accident, use impossible layers, or ignore how stress travels. In the world, a printer nozzle has a size, a resin blurs as light and chemistry spread, fabric plies need manufacturable thickness, architectural panels must carry load, and a virtual object can feel real only if some nearby physical object can stand in for it. The shared problem is not just making a shape. It is converting intent into a build plan that respects matter. Each paper asks what must stay true during that conversion: a composite should become stiffer, a freeform surface should keep its look while lowering stress, a triangle surface should stop crossing through itself, a filament printer should follow continuous bead paths, a VR touch target should match a real object, and a holographic printer should deposit enough curing dose in the right tiny places. The family exists because fabrication exposes every hidden lie in a digital model.
naive_failure: A smart beginner would first separate design from making. Draw the best-looking surface, then panelize it. Pick a strong composite layout, then cut fabric layers afterward. Slice a print into ordinary flat layers, then ask the nozzle to follow them. Remove surface crossings by pushing apart only the visibly colliding triangles. For touch in VR, print a matching prop or use visual feedback alone. For holographic printing, compute the light pattern and ignore how the resin keeps reacting after light arrives. These ideas fail because physical constraints are coupled. Changing a panel changes stress elsewhere. A fabric boundary changes stiffness across neighboring layers. A local untangle can create a larger knot. A nozzle path must preserve bead thickness, avoid collisions, and keep moving. A room object must match shape, position, and touch qualities. In resin, optics and chemistry blur together.
mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical principle is to turn fabrication into a scored agreement among many promises. A promise can be geometric: the surface should stay close to the intended form, should not pass through itself, and should be split into usable panels or layers. A promise can be mechanical: stress should be lowered, stiffness should rise, and material directions should carry force well. A promise can be machine-related: the filament bead should keep nearly constant thickness, the tool should not collide, and non-printing travel should be small. A promise can be sensory or chemical: a real object should match a virtual touch target, or a hologram should create a dose pattern that survives light bending and inhibitor diffusion. The method then adjusts the design, layer fields, paths, surface positions, hologram sequence, or object match to reduce the measured violations. This is optimization, meaning repeated score-and-adjust search, but the score is not abstract. It is a checklist of what would break in fabrication. The key tradeoff is design freedom versus physical obedience: enough freedom to improve shape, touch, stiffness, or resolution, but enough obedience that the result can actually be made or used.
why_math_matters: The math matters because fabrication constraints are spread out, not isolated. Stress is global: a weak region may be caused by panel choices far away because load travels through the whole shell. Composite layers are directional: a fabric ply can be strong along one direction and weaker across another, so partial layer boundaries change how force moves between layers. Self-intersection is also global. A triangle surface, meaning a skin made of many flat patches, can be locally separated in one place yet still folded through itself as a whole. Filament printing is path-based: every point on a layer affects the next point because the nozzle must move continuously with a fixed bead profile. Holographic resin printing is coupled through light waves and chemistry: the projected phase pattern bends light, while curing and inhibitor diffusion smear the final solid. ProXeek uses the same logic in a different material setting: the physical room already contains objects, but a match is useful only when several constraints agree at once. Mathematics gives these papers a way to see long-range consequences before a machine or user exposes the mistake.
paper_family: The papers are siblings because each replaces an after-the-fact repair step with a coupled making plan. Co-Optimization of Structure and Manufacturable Semi-Continuous Layers for Laminated Composites does not first choose a shape and later decide fabric plies. It adjusts structure and manufacturable partial layers together, modeling how layer boundaries change directional mechanical behavior, and reports higher stiffness than planar ply counterparts. Stress-Aware Panelization makes a similar move for architecture: instead of panelizing a freeform surface and only then checking strength, it lets stress analysis influence the surface flow while preserving design intent. Untangling Surfaces handles the prerequisite for many fabrication pipelines: the digital skin must be embedded, meaning it occupies space without crossing through itself, so the method uses both broad shape repulsion and local triangle-level penalties. AtomSlicer turns multi-axis filament printing into a path agreement problem, preserving orientation fields, near-constant layer thickness, continuous toolpaths, and collision avoidance, or reporting that the request cannot be fabricated. Single-View Holographic Volumetric 3D Printing couples wave optics with resin chemistry so the light plan pre-compensates for chemical blur. ProXeek broadens fabrication into opportunistic touch: rather than making a prop, it matches virtual interactables to real objects already in the room.
what_changed: The 2026 pattern is that fabrication papers are moving from shape-first pipelines toward constraint-first pipelines. The evidence emphasizes joint design and manufacturing instead of cleanup after design is frozen. Composite layout, panel stress, surface untangling, multi-axis slicing, holographic curing, and VR haptic proxy selection all treat fabrication limits as part of the main computation. Another change is stronger honesty about feasibility. AtomSlicer preserves user or solver-defined fields and reports non-fabricability rather than quietly changing the request. The holographic printer models both optics and chemistry rather than only the projected light. ProXeek compares real room objects against touch constraints instead of assuming a custom printed replica is the best physical answer.
limits: These results depend on the chosen physical models and inputs. Composite design assumes the layer field, stiffness model, and manufacturing objectives describe the real fabric plies well enough. Stress-aware panelization depends on the shell model, stress objective, and architectural shapes tested. Untangling assumes the surface representation can be moved without changing connectivity and that repulsion energies capture the relevant crossings. AtomSlicer assumes supplied orientation fields, bead profile, and machine collision checks match the printer. Holographic volumetric printing is shown on small volumes and simple structures, with simplified photochemistry. ProXeek depends on headset snapshots, annotations, language-model reasoning, and available room objects. The evidence reports selected validations, not universal guarantees across all materials, printers, rooms, scales, noise levels, or manufacturing tolerances.
